title: AI investment, govt borrowing drive global cost of capital higher: Goldman Sachs
content:
New Delhi [India], September 19 (ANI): Rising spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and higher government borrowing are pushing up the global cost of capital, as companies raise more debt and equity to fund investment while governments increase borrowing for infrastructure, energy security and defence, Goldman Sachs said in a report.
The report said the two major themes dominating investor discussions -- AI and rising interest rates -- are increasingly linked as demand for capital rises across both the private and public sectors.
“In the private sector a surge in capex spending to fund AI infrastructure has eaten into free cash flow and forced companies to raise more in debt and equity markets,” the report said, adding that higher government borrowing and inflationary pressures from energy prices have also contributed to the rise in funding costs.
Goldman Sachs noted that 30-year government bond yields in Germany and Japan were close to zero as recently as 2022, while higher yields and greater uncertainty around geopolitics and AI have since increased the cost of capital.
The impact is already visible in corporate financing. Capital expenditure by AA-rated issuers rose 65 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter, marking the 10th consecutive quarter in which aggregate AA capex growth exceeded 35 per cent, the report said.
Companies have also increasingly turned to credit and equity markets to fund the investment. US convertible bond issuance has reached USD 135 billion so far this year, with AI-related borrowers accounting for 44 per cent of the total, according to the report.
Goldman Sachs’ credit team has raised its full-year US investment-grade gross issuance forecast by USD 200 billion to USD 2.3 trillion, with AI-related issuers accounting for about a quarter of US investment-grade gross supply this year.
The report added that higher funding costs could put pressure on equities if earnings growth slows. While technology valuations have moderated and are below their 20-year median globally, the key risk is whether the current strength in earnings proves sustainable.
“Nonetheless, any slowdown in profit growth, in an environment of a much higher cost of capital, could put downward pressure on equity prices,” the report said.
Goldman Sachs expects earnings growth and nominal GDP growth to remain important drivers of equity performance, while noting that higher bond yields are likely to limit further valuation expansion. The bank said opportunities were broadening across geographies, sectors and factors as earnings growth becomes more widely distributed. (ANI)

report.summary: Goldman Sachs says AI infrastructure spending and higher government borrowing are driving up the global cost of capital, reshaping corporate financing and equity risks.
report.background: After years of ultra-low rates, the global cost of capital began rising in 2022 as central banks tightened policy. Now two forces are reinforcing each other: massive private investment in AI data centers, chips and cloud capacity, and heavy government borrowing for infrastructure, energy security and defence. AI capex has consumed free cash flow at many firms, pushing them to issue more debt and equity. At the same time, higher sovereign yields and energy-driven inflation have lifted hurdle rates across markets. Goldman notes that 30-year German and Japanese bond yields were near zero as recently as 2022. The result is a more expensive funding environment that links the AI boom directly to interest-rate and credit-market conditions.
key_points: AI infrastructure capex is straining corporate balance sheets. Goldman says capital expenditure by AA-rated issuers rose 65% year-on-year in Q2, the 10th straight quarter of aggregate AA capex growth above 35%. With free cash flow eaten up, companies are raising more debt and equity, tying the AI investment cycle to credit markets and making funding costs a central investor concern.

Government borrowing is adding to the pressure. Higher issuance for infrastructure, energy security and defence, alongside energy-driven inflation, has pushed sovereign yields up. Goldman notes 30-year German and Japanese government bond yields were close to zero in 2022; today's higher yields and geopolitical uncertainty have raised the global cost of capital.

AI borrowers now dominate parts of the issuance market. US convertible bond issuance reached $135 billion this year, with AI-related borrowers at 44%. Goldman raised its full-year US investment-grade gross issuance forecast by $200 billion to $2.3 trillion, with AI-related issuers about a quarter of supply.

Equity markets face a sustainability test. Tech valuations have moderated and sit below their 20-year global median, but Goldman warns that any slowdown in profit growth, in a much higher cost-of-capital environment, could pressure equity prices. Higher bond yields are likely to limit further valuation expansion.

Opportunities may broaden beyond US tech. Goldman expects earnings and nominal GDP growth to remain key equity drivers, with opportunities spreading across geographies, sectors and factors as earnings growth becomes more widely distributed. That shifts focus from pure valuation expansion to fundamental earnings delivery.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report signals that capital is still available but no longer cheap. Large cloud and chip firms can fund capex from cash flow, but rising debt costs may slow marginal projects and force sharper ROI scrutiny. AI startups could face higher funding hurdles, favoring incumbents and consolidation. Developers may see continued pressure on compute and cloud pricing, though efficiency gains and open models could offset some costs. Regular users may benefit from better AI products if investment pays off, but could face higher prices if firms pass on financing costs; broader higher rates also affect loans, mortgages and equity portfolios. The key risk is an earnings slowdown colliding with expensive capital, which could rattle tech-heavy markets and cool the AI investment cycle.
report.tools: To track these trends, use FRED (fred.stlouisfed.org) for sovereign yields and inflation, SEC EDGAR full-text search for AI-related capex, debt and convertible issuance, and OpenBB or yfinance for market and earnings data. Goldman Sachs Insights publishes the underlying research notes. For open-source macro dashboards, explore OpenBB Platform and BIS statistics on credit and cross-border lending.
